layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract—In the present study, a 316 wire loop electrode system has been shown to give good

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reproducible results in a variety of halide environments. An unusual feature of these results is the fact that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: under all experimental conditions studied, the Br~ ion is found to be considerably (approx. 200 mV) more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aggressive than the Cl ion in terms of oxide stability. This trend is also maintained with steels 302 and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 304L. The presence of SO⁻ ions in the halide electrolyte does not alter this order, nor does chemical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pre-treatment in acid solutions prior to pitting potential determinations. Pitting potentials measured for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 316 wire loop samples are considerably more noble than those measured for samples of 316 cut from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bar or sheet material. It is tentatively suggested that this order of oxide stability may be due to the superior

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ability of Cl~ to adsorb at flaws in the developing oxide film, the wire loop samples containing fewer such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: flaws.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The breakdown of passivity, which leads to localized corrosion, is a very common

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type of failure encountered with stainless steels. The pitting and crevice corrosion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behaviour of stainless steels has been studied extensively in environments containing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aggressive ions similar to those found in their operating conditions, and reviewed by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a number of workers.1-6 Most work however has been done in solutions containing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cl" as the aggressive ion. This is presumably because chlorides are most commonly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encountered in environments such as sea-water, pulp and paper processing and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: chemical plants in general. It is believed that Cl~ ions are the most aggressive anions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the pitting and crevice corrosion attack on stainless steels.7,8

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experimental arrangements or procedures for the determination of the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: susceptibility of stainless steels in halide environments are many and varied.9,10 The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accuracy and reliability of such tests however, depend very markedly on the working

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assemblies used, one of the most important considerations being that the electrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system should be crevice-free. This is particularly so if the tests are to be conducted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over extended periods of time or at elevated temperatures. Pitting susceptibility

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results obtained for steel samples mounted in epoxy resin, waxed samples or those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involving O-ring seals must therefore always be treated with a certain amount of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: care, particularly in their extrapolation to industrial situations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is of considerable importance therefore that new, crevice-free electrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: systems be developed and tested. In these laboratories the crevice-free electrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In an attempt to find an easier and more rapid test procedure various other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: crevice-free electrode assemblies were examined. The present communication

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bromide and chloride solutions.

layout_dets.text: EXPERIMENTAL METHOD

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Unless otherwise stated the test electrodes were made from 0.25 mm wire looped to a diameter of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 25 mm. The electrodes were attached to the holder as indicated in Fig. 1b and immersed to half distance to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: give an exposed surface area of 0.32 cm². Apart from a washing in distilled water and methanol, the wires

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were used in the as-received state. Test solutions were prepared from reagent grade chemicals and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distilled water and the pH value was adjusted using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or NaOH as required. The oxygen content of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the test solutions was reduced to a negligible value by bubbling nitrogen through them for a period of 24 h.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: All electrochemical measurements were performed in a conventional three electrode glass cell, purged

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with nitrogen during each experiment, the potential controlled and the currents measured using a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Princeton Applied Research Model 273 potentiostat/galvanostat and associated Model 342 Softcorr

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion measurement software. Prior to each measurement the sample was introduced into the test

layout_dets.text: DISCUSSION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As indicated in the introduction, the object of this work was to evaluate the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: performance of the crevice-free electrode assembly in order to carry out routine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion tests in various halide solutions. The present wire loop electrode system

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: works very well in this context, giving good reproducible results for repeated tests

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over a wide range of experimental conditions. Within these sets of test results, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one factor which perhaps might mitigate against the system, and indeed the one most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: difficult to explain is the order of aggressiveness in the Cl~ and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions. Results

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with this order of aggressiveness are not indeed unique,19,20 with electrode systems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of other conformations.

layout_dets.text: increase in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing solutions is considerably less than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those observed for the solutions containing

layout_dets.text: . Surface treatments of this kind are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: considered

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to remove sites on the steel surface (sulphides and other inclusions),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which might otherwise lead to defects in the developing surface oxide. These defect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sites are believed to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the areas where pit initiation takes place in halide solutions,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probably as a result of the higher field strengths associated with such flaws. Addition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of inhibitors to solutions containing halide ions, can result in preferential adsorption

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of inhibitor ions at these flaws13 thus preventing attack by halide. However, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indicated in Fig. 8, while the presence of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion does lead to a considerable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increase in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: value for the 316 steel wire the order of oxide stability is still

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: maintained. It is also clear from the data in Fig. 6, that in solutions containing both

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions, small amounts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.text: potential down to values close to those measured in solutions containing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Attack by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion at the oxide surface would seem therefore to be relatively

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independent of the Cl⁻ presence or concentration.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It has been postulated²³ that the potential of zero charge

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the surface

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: oxide in halide solutions, can in many instances be related to the specific potential at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which pitting attack on the oxide commences. For this work it is very difficult to see

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: why the order of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values should reverse for the wire sample relative to those

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cut from bar or sheet.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In a further attempt to rationalize the order of aggressivity the alloy constituents

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the 316 steel specimens were considered further. Iron, nickel and molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were commercially available in wire form of similar thickness to the steel and these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were tested in solutions similar to those used for the 316 electrodes. Results for these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: metals are shown in Fig. 9, where the potential is plotted versus pH for 1.0 M NaCl

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and 1.0 M NaBr solutions. Where definite pitting potentials were not evident on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polarization plots, the potential corresponding to an anodic current of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was used in the plots. These data show the usual trends for these metals in halide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions of varying pH.13 For Fe, Ni and Mo the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is found to be the more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aggressive anion although not by a very substantial margin. Pitting potentials

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: measured for a flat sample of Cr metal in 1.0 M NaCl and 1.0 M NaBr, pH 2.5

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions were 856 and 866 mV, respectively, again the usual trend. Included in Fig. 9

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also are some results for an 80% Ni:20% Cr wire sample. Here the order of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aggressiveness is found to be similar to that for the 316 steel sample, but by a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: considerably reduced amount. While the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values for this wire sample are very

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: much higher than those for pure Ni it would seem fair to say that it is not the overall

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: composition of the steel alloy which determines this order of oxide stability. Other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: factors must be considered.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It has been shown²⁴ that the ability of halide ions to adsorb on metal or oxide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surfaces normally increases in the order

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which is also the order

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of increasing ionic radius. For I− and F~ solutions the verification of this sequence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aggressiveness for stainless steels is difficult, due to the occurrence of secondary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: processes.12 For

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions, it is fair to say, that stainless steels, except on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quite rare occasions show the reverse order of pitting tendencies. Pitting studies on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ti metal and some of its alloys²⁵ and also on Ta metal,26 have yielded results which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: agree with the above order of adsorption ability.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The exact meaning of, or the precise factors which govern the pitting tendency of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steels in these halide solutions would thus seem difficult to rationalize.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From the results so far presented two interesting points emerge which might, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part at least, give some further insights into the observed order or pitting suscepti-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bility. These are: (i)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values determined for the wire loop electrode in the bromide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions studied are reasonably similar to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values obtained for 316L and 304

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electrodes12,13 cut from steel bar. In chloride solutions, however,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: measured using the wire loop system are considerably higher than those obtained for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 316L and 304 samples cut from steel bar and indeed for 316 sheet metal²7 samples;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (ii) as indicated in Table 2, the improvement in the pitting potential, observed after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the various surface treatments shown, is considerably less pronounced for tests in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solutions, than those observed for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ones. It would seem reasonable to assume

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the basis of these two observations that the anomalous behaviour observed in this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: instance is associated with attack on the oxide surface by the Cl− ion.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In a recent paper, Burstein and Pistorius28 reported a pitting potential of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A crevice-free electrode for stainless steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 550 mV(SCE) for a type 304 steel, immersed in solution (1.0 M NaCl, pH 0.7) in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form of 50 μm wire electrodes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Indeed for some 25% of these wire electrodes, breakdown did not occur until at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least 850 mV. These values are considerably higher than those obtained with 304

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steel samples cut from sheet or bar in similar chloride solutions. These authors

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suggest that the very high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values obtained with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electrodes may be as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: result of the strong refining effect of the wire-drawing process on malleable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inclusions (such as sulphides) or other pit nucleation sites. All this could perhaps

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suggest that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion has a much greater tendency to adsorb at surface inclusions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such as sulphides than the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion. Thus the greater the population of these surface

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: defects, the easier it is for pit initiation to occur. The lower the population density, as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is the case for the wire loop samples, the more difficult it is for attack to initiate, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: so the real adsorption ability of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions comes into play. This may

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: indeed explain the wide variation in pitting potential values measured by different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: workers for the same steel type in given halide solutions. Perhaps on a surface free of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: inclusions or other defects the order of film breakdown would reflect that of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adsorption tendencies very closely. This ability of Cl− to adsorb at flaws, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generate conditions leading to metastable pit formation, is very evident from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentiostatic current-time plots shown in Fig. 10a and b. In Fig. 10a the decay

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: profile is for the wire loop in a 1.0 M NaCl, pH 2.5 solution, recorded at a potential of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 400 mV(SCE), while in Fig. 10b the decay profile is for the 316 wire loop in a 1.0 M

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: NaBr, pH 2.5 solution, the potential in this case being 300 mV(SCE). Thus while the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wire loop samples may have a reduced population density of surface flaws, it is clear

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that in the Cl− solution the greatest number of pit initiation events take place. This is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: even more striking, since the potential chosen for the measurement in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution is more than 120 mV removed from the potentiodynamically determined

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting potential while for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution the potential chosen is only approxi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mately 25 mV from the pitting potential. Why attack by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ion on the oxide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covered metal, seems less dependent on the presence of surface inclusions or flaws is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not immediately obvious and is the subject of further study.
